query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy (HEA), brittle behavior emerges due to the formation of nanoscale ordered precipitates at grain boundaries under prolonged thermal exposure, which disrupts the local compositional complexity and induces embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase high-entropy alloy with uniform compositional complexity and no detectable grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to prolonged thermal exposure at elevated temperatures within the service range of the material.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure at temperatures between 600°C and 900°C for durations ranging from 10 to 100 hours, under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale ordered precipitates at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal exposure promotes local diffusion and segregation of specific elements to grain boundaries, leading to the nucleation and growth of ordered precipitates. These precipitates disrupt the compositional complexity and reduce the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries, resulting in brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline single-phase state, the thermally exposed HEA will exhibit reduced fracture toughness and increased intergranular fracture under tensile or impact loading.
generation.baseline: The fracture toughness and fracture mode of the as-prepared single-phase HEA before thermal exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for HEAs with a single-phase microstructure at room temperature and service temperatures up to 900°C, but not for alloys with pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates or significant phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: The specific elements and compositions that are most prone to grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation are not identified, and the kinetics of the process may vary significantly among different HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the single-phase HEA and subject them to thermal exposure at 600°C, 750°C, and 900°C for 10, 50, and 100 hours. Perform microstructural analysis using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to detect grain-boundary precipitates. Conduct fracture toughness tests and fractography to assess changes in mechanical behavior and fracture mode.
measurements: Presence and composition of grain-boundary precipitates (TEM, APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no grain-boundary precipitates are observed after thermal exposure, or if fracture toughness and fracture mode remain unchanged compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
